ethiopia.content: UK warns citizens against non-essential travel to Moyale amid Ethiopia clashes - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME SECURITY UK warns citizens against non-essential travel to Moyale amid Ethiopia clashes Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ by FELIX KIPKEMOI Saturday November 7, 2026 British Embassy in Nairobi/FILE The United Kingdom has cautioned its citizens against making non-essential travel to Moyale town and its environs in light of the ongoing cross-border violence that has caused death, injuries and displaced thousands. ‎In an updated travel advisory issued on November 6, UK's Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) said the warning reflected its assessment of the deteriorating security situation and reports of cross-border incidents affecting the Kenyan side of the border with Ethiopia. ‎ advertisements The advisory covers Moyale town and an area extending five kilometres around it, including the border with Ethiopia. ‎"The travel advice update for Moyale town advises against all but essential travel. This reflects our assessment of the security situation and reports of cross-border incidents affecting the Kenyan side of the border," the FCDO said. ‎The warning comes as Kenyan security agencies step up operations along the border following fighting that erupted on October 22 in neighbouring Ethiopia. ‎Inspector General of Police Douglas Kanja on Thursday, November 5, ordered the deployment of additional officers to reinforce security in the border town. ‎During a security assessment visit, Kanja said officers had been directed to strengthen surveillance and remain on high alert to prevent the violence from spilling further into Kenya. ‎He also assured residents that the government was committed to protecting lives and property amid growing fears over stray ammunition. ‎ Kanja disclosed that two women, one Kenyan and another Ethiopian, had died after being struck by stray bullets, while several others had sustained injuries. ‎"One life has been lost on the Kenyan side after a woman was hit by a stray bullet on the neck. We have also recorded injuries arising from stray bullets. The best way to address this situation is to ensure the conflict is resolved quickly," he said. ‎The police chief also disclosed that approximately 10,000 displaced people were still living in temporary shelters and public institutions around Moyale, as humanitarian agencies continued providing emergency assistance. ‎The fighting has disrupted cross-border trade, movement of goods and services and electricity supply to Moyale, which relies heavily on power from Ethiopia. ‎The British advisory further maintains restrictions on several other parts of northern and eastern Kenya over terrorism threats, particularly from the Somalia-based al Shabaab militant group.‎ The FCDO advises against all travel to Mandera county, parts of Wajir county, most of Garissa county and parts of Lamu county. ‎It also advises against all but essential travel to Garissa Town, parts of Tana River county and sections of the coastline. ‎The latest warning adds to concerns over the security situation in the Horn of Africa, where instability across national borders continues to affect communities, trade and movement of people. ‎The FCDO said its travel advice is regularly reviewed as security conditions change, urging British nationals to consult its guidance before travelling. ‎The warning does not amount to a general travel ban on Kenya but specifically targets areas assessed to face heightened security risks. ethiopia.summary: The UK government has issued a travel advisory warning its citizens against non-essential travel to Moyale, Kenya, due to escalating violence linked to cross-border clashes with Ethiopia. The advisory, released on November 6 by the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO), highlights the deteriorating security situation, including reports of incidents affecting the Kenyan side of the border. The advisory specifically targets Moyale and a five-kilometer radius around it. In response to the violence, which began on October 22, Kenyan authorities have intensified security measures, deploying additional officers to the area. Tragically, stray bullets have resulted in casualties, including the death of a woman in Kenya. Approximately 10,000 people have been displaced and are currently in temporary shelters. The FCDO's advisory also maintains travel restrictions in other parts of northern and eastern Kenya due to terrorism threats, particularly from the al Shabaab militant group. The situation reflects broader instability in the Horn of Africa.

ethiopia.content: Ethiopia, Eritrea and the Politics of Strategic Depth – HORN REVIEW Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us Search Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us 2026-11-07 Ethiopia, Eritrea and the Politics of Strategic Depth 0 Comments Eritrea remains a structural challenge to Ethiopia’s national security. The present relationship between the two countries is defined by escalating tensions, in which Asmara, consistent with its broader and long-standing calculation that a stable Ethiopia constitutes a threat, has cultivated alliances with Ethiopia’s diverse rebel groups in order to weaken Addis Ababa. What shape the Ethiopian response to that threat should take has been a matter of debate. Addis Ababa has taken steps to counter the rebels themselves, while Eritrea’s broader antagonism remains unaddressed, a question of considerable sensitivity and complexity because it belongs to the realm of interstate dynamics. Nonetheless, Ethiopia possesses an array of options for dealing with the Eritrean threat, one being the establishment of strategic depth of its own. In Tigray, Ethiopia’s northern region, Eritrea’s proxy penetration of Ethiopia’s security space has centred on the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) , which has thus far been the most prominent and capable of the rebel groups inside Ethiopia. Before a counteroffensive by the Ethiopian National Defence Force (ENDF) forced it into a crushing retreat to Tigray’s countryside, the TPLF had served as the linchpin of Eritrea’s buffer-zone strategy. The shared border between Tigray and Eritrea allowed the relationship between the PFDJ/EPLF (Eritrea’s ruling regime) and the TPLF to develop, and the regime to invest in the Tigrayan front, effectively establishing strategic depth inside Ethiopia. The TPLF is one element among several in Eritrea’s strategy. The Ethiopia-Eritrea border extends beyond Tigray and cuts through the homeland of the Afar people, and Eritrea has also exploited the politics of Ethiopia’s Afar region to its apparent advantage. A smaller but long-standing rebel group, the Afar Revolutionary Democratic Unity Front (ARDUF), which has regarded Addis Ababa as an adversary, saw its leadership travel to Eritrea in 2025 , where it reorganised the front. Ahead of the TPLF offensive of 23 September, the ARDUF became part of a broader alliance of rebels and joined the fighting itself, primarily in Ethiopia’s Afar region. The rebel alliance, formalised as the “Alliance for Survival”, was at least in part engineered by Asmara, whose reach extends beyond the TPLF and the ARDUF to the rebels of the Amhara and Oromia regions, which, alongside the TPLF, make up the coalition’s three core members. Where the Ethiopia-Eritrea border served as the bridge for Eritrea’s strategic depth in Tigray, reaching the Amhara region and the Fano rebellion, specifically the grouping under the Amhara Fano National Movement (AFNM), and by extension the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) in Oromia, has been orchestrated by distinct means. In addition to the links among the rebels themselves (such as between the AFNM and the TPLF), Asmara has found its previously established relationships, formed as host to Ethiopian rebels under the previous Ethiopian administration, useful. It comes as no surprise that Asmara is able to reach the OLA leadership, a group that had maintained a prolonged presence in Eritrea, and some figures within the AFNM, including its leader, Zemene Kassie, who has a history with the Eritrean regime from his time in the Ginbot 7 rebel group . More concretely, Eritrea has been able to reach the AFNM materially through the strategic exploitation of Sudan and the instability produced by its civil war. Through its broad involvement in Sudan’s war , Eritrea has hosted meetings between the rebels and its representatives and even supplied logistics directly to the AFNM, as multiple reports have revealed. Since late September, the dynamics on the ground between Ethiopia and Eritrea and its proxies have shifted radically. They reveal that the Eritrean buffer zone has been largely degraded, if not wholly dismantled. Ethiopian forces now maintain a steady presence on the Ethiopian side of the border with Eritrea, and the rebels, even if not permanently neutralised, have weakened in their ability to tie down the Ethiopian security establishment, which enjoys a marked asymmetry in capacity relative to Eritrea’s limited military prowess. The Eritrean threat nonetheless persists. The “Alliance for Survival” still maintains its goal of overthrowing the government in Addis Ababa and destabilising Ethiopia, albeit with more modest capacity than it originally intended. More structurally, the PFDJ’s enduring strategic thought, which Ethiopia’s foreign minister has described as equating Ethiopia’s instability and state weakness with Eritrea’s own security and longevity, will ensure Asmara remains a permanent dilemma for the Ethiopian security establishment. To meet that challenge, Addis Ababa has a range of options to consider, which could take the form of a direct offensive against Asmara itself, such as targeting the apparatus of the regime so as to render it incapable of implementing its strategy, while avoiding an all-out confrontation, which would foment complex dynamics in turn. It could also establish a degree of strategic depth that would constrain Asmara’s ability to threaten Ethiopia’s national security. For one, the option of a military approach to establishing such depth, which would mean the creation of a buffer zone inside Eritrea itself, remains available and falls under the rationale of self-defence granted to Ethiopia by international law. This rationale rests on two major considerations. The first is that the Eritrean Defence Forces (EDF) displayed their appetite for direct confrontation during the proxies’ September offensive. As Eritrea’s buffer zone in Tigray broke down, EDF personnel made deep incursions into the region (having already established a presence in border towns), as recorded by various reports and asserted by Addis Ababa itself. Although they were pushed back quickly, the incursion proved that the possibility of direct EDF attacks on Ethiopian forces remains high. The second is the TPLF factor in this threat. Although the ENDF has largely re-established its positions along Ethiopia’s border, it may face the Front from Eritrean territory as well as from the Tigrayan countryside. Such a threat is plausible given Eritrea’s past willingness to open its territory to Ethiopian rebels and the TPLF’s own receding fighting capability inside Tigray, which makes the prospect of the group using Eritrea as a safe haven and a launchpad for its fight against the Ethiopian government more likely. Broader forms of strategic depth vis-à-vis the Eritrean regime could also enter Ethiopia’s defence calculus. One strategy employed by the PFDJ leadership has been a diplomatic and media push to recast Eritrea’s military posture as defensive while portraying Ethiopia as harbouring aggressive intent. This has been visible in the diplomatic offensive by its senior envoys, including the Eritrean foreign minister, directed at the United Nations, the African Union and several Western capitals, which has characterised Ethiopia’s interests, particularly in the Red Sea, as “expansionist” and invoked international law and narratives of sovereignty. Eritrea’s media campaign has followed the same trajectory. Concealing Eritrea’s proxy mobilisation and direct incursions, it has pushed narratives of Ethiopian aggression to undermine Ethiopia’s standing amongst the international community. Addis Ababa has ground to gain on the diplomatic front. It has already made its position clear to the United Nations and through bilateral channels. Beyond asserting its defensive position, it could go further to lay bare the hostile strategy within Asmara’s rationale, and to expose its role in the formation of the rebel coalition. The logic of strategic depth, which should also be comprehensive in addressing Eritrea’s various avenues of projection, such as its influence over Sudan and its activities there, is likely the way forward. The fundamental posture of the Eritrean regime, and its hostility toward a stable and secure Ethiopia, remain a central threat to Ethiopia’s national security, one broader in scope than the rapidly shifting dynamics on the ground. ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia faces a persistent national security challenge from Eritrea, which has fostered alliances with various Ethiopian rebel groups to destabilize the government in Addis Ababa. The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) has been a key player in this strategy, serving as a proxy for Eritrea until a recent Ethiopian counteroffensive forced it into retreat. Eritrea's influence extends beyond Tigray, involving the Afar Revolutionary Democratic Unity Front (ARDUF) and other regional rebels, forming a coalition known as the "Alliance for Survival." Despite recent military successes, the threat from Eritrea and its proxies remains, as they continue to seek to undermine Ethiopia's stability. Ethiopia has several strategic options to counter this threat, including establishing a buffer zone within Eritrea and enhancing its diplomatic efforts to expose Eritrea's aggressive posture. The ongoing dynamics highlight the complexity of Ethiopia's security landscape and the enduring challenge posed by Eritrea's strategic ambitions. (159 words)

ethiopia.summary: Kenya's Inspector General of Police, Douglas Kanja, announced on November 5 that the country is actively engaging with Ethiopia to resolve the ongoing conflict in Moyale. During a high-level security visit to the region, Kanja emphasized the importance of collaboration between the two nations to restore peace and stability. The Moyale conflict has raised concerns over security and the well-being of residents in the border area. Kanja's delegation included various security officials who assessed the situation and discussed strategies to mitigate tensions. The Kenyan government is committed to fostering dialogue and cooperation with Ethiopian authorities to address the underlying issues contributing to the unrest. Both countries recognize the need for a coordinated approach to ensure lasting peace and prevent further escalation of violence in the region. This initiative reflects Kenya's broader commitment to regional stability and security cooperation with its neighbors.

ethiopia.title: Somalia warns Ethiopia unrest could weaken AUSSOM security operations - Hiiraan Online
ethiopia.content: Somalia warns Ethiopia unrest could weaken AUSSOM security operations - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME SECURITY Somalia warns Ethiopia unrest could weaken AUSSOM security operations Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Thursday November 5, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) - Somalia warned Thursday that worsening political and security instability in neighboring Ethiopia could affect security operations inside Somalia, including the African Union mission fighting al-Shabab. State Minister for Foreign Affairs Ali Mohamed Omar Balcad, told TRT World that Ethiopia’s stability was directly linked to Somalia’s security because of the countries’ long shared border and deep economic, social and historical ties. advertisements He warned that prolonged unrest inside Ethiopia could affect Ethiopian troops serving in the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM), potentially forcing Addis Ababa to reduce or withdraw forces to respond to domestic security pressures. Ethiopian troops remain a significant component of AUSSOM. The African Union approved a contingent of about 2,500 Ethiopian troops for the mission, alongside forces from Uganda, Kenya, Djibouti and Egypt. Ethiopia has also deployed additional forces in Somalia under bilateral arrangements. The African Union Peace and Security Council praised both Ethiopia and Uganda in February for sending additional troops as a temporary measure to address Somalia’s security situation. In September, the Ethiopian National Defence Force completed a major rotation of troops serving in AUSSOM’s Sector 4, which covers parts of central Somalia. New Ethiopian personnel replaced troops stationed in Beletweyne and Halgan after a three-year deployment. Ali Balcad cautioned that a deterioration of Ethiopia’s internal security could therefore have consequences for Somalia if Ethiopian forces were required to redeploy home or became less able to support operations against al-Shabab. Such a development could create additional pressure on Somali security forces at a time when the federal government and AUSSOM are already trying to gradually transfer responsibility for national security to Somali institutions. The warning comes amid renewed fighting inside Ethiopia. Conflict between Ethiopia’s federal government and forces linked to the Tigray People’s Liberation Front erupted again in September, effectively breaking down the 2022 Pretoria peace agreement that ended a devastating two-year war. Ethiopian government forces later retook much of Tigray, including the regional capital, Mekelle. Violence has also continued in Amhara. Drone strikes on a displacement camp there killed at least 15 people, including children, on Oct. 30, according to people involved in rescue efforts who spoke to Reuters. It was not clear who carried out the attack. Regional tensions have also increased between Ethiopia and Eritrea, with the two countries severing diplomatic relations and reports of Eritrean troops entering northern Ethiopia during the renewed Tigray fighting. Ali Balcad also warned that violence inside Ethiopia could directly affect ethnic Somalis living in Ethiopia’s Somali Region, which borders Somalia. AUSSOM replaced the African Union Transition Mission in Somalia at the beginning of 2025. Its mandate includes supporting Somali forces in operations against al-Shabab, protecting key population centers and infrastructure, and helping Somali security institutions assume greater responsibility for national security. The African Union has repeatedly warned that any changes to the mission must be carefully coordinated to prevent security gaps, particularly while al-Shabab retains the ability to carry out major attacks across southern and central Somalia. ethiopia.content: UK Tightens Kenya Travel Advice After Border Security Fears Skip to content Home The Network Contact Subscribe Home The Network Contact Subscribe News UK Tightens Kenya Travel Advice After Border Security Fears The UK has updated its Kenya travel advice, expanding “avoid travel” areas near the Ethiopia border and reminding tourists that insurance may be void if they ignore alerts. Jolyon Zivkov · Nov 7, 2026 The Traveler contains affiliate links. If you click through and make a purchase, we may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. Table of contents More news on this day New U.S. Warnings Raise Stakes for Winter Dubai Stopovers Lender Seizes Control of Stranded Villa Vie Odyssey Ship UK Tightens Kenya Travel Advice After Moyale Border Unrest The United Kingdom has issued an updated travel warning for Kenya, extending caution around the Ethiopia border and reiterating restrictions along the frontier with Somalia, in a move that could affect winter safaris and coastal holidays for British travelers. Get the latest news straight to your inbox! What Has Changed in the UK’s Kenya Travel Advice According to the latest update on the UK government’s Kenya travel advice page dated 6 November 2026, the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) has expanded its warning to cover Moyale Town and a 5‑kilometre radius around it on the Kenyan side of the border with Ethiopia. Publicly available information states that the FCDO now advises against all but essential travel to this pocket of northern Kenya, citing security concerns linked to unrest across the border. This adjustment builds on an earlier revision at the end of October 2026, when the FCDO first updated its sections on the Kenya–Ethiopia border under “Warnings and insurance” and “Regional risks.” The core of the travel advice remains unchanged: there is a long‑standing warning against all travel to parts of the north‑east and areas along the Kenyan‑Somali frontier, and against all but essential travel to some surrounding districts. The new wording does not amount to a nationwide escalation, but it tightens advice around a specific cross‑border flashpoint at a time when regional tensions and sporadic violence in southern Ethiopia have been widely reported. The revision comes as many British visitors are finalizing trips for the December and January peak safari season, prompting renewed scrutiny of how travel advisories could influence itineraries. Travel guidance also continues to underline that terrorism and crime remain significant concerns in some parts of Kenya. The advisory highlights what it describes as a high threat of terrorist attack, referencing the activity of groups such as Al Shabaab and their history of targeting Kenyan security forces, public places and infrastructure. Areas Most Affected by the UK Warning The updated advice preserves a clear geographical distinction between regions that are heavily restricted and areas considered suitable for normal travel. The strictest warning, advising against all travel, still applies to swathes of territory near the border with Somalia, including Mandera County, much of Wajir County close to the frontier and parts of Garissa County outside Garissa Town and certain corridors further inland. In addition, the FCDO advises against all but essential travel to several other localities, including parts of Lamu County on the northern coast and interior stretches of Tana River and Kilifi counties. These areas have periodically seen security incidents over the past decade, and the advice reflects a long‑term pattern rather than a sudden shift. The November 2026 notice draws particular attention to Moyale, a key crossing point on the A2 highway connecting northern Kenya to Ethiopia. Regional risk pages note that violence in the Ethiopian town of Moyale since October has had spillover effects near the border, leading the UK to tighten its stance on movement in and around the Kenyan side of the crossing. Popular tourist hubs, including Nairobi, the Maasai Mara, Amboseli, Laikipia conservancies and the main coastal resorts around Mombasa, Diani and Watamu, remain outside the no‑go zones. The FCDO states that most of Kenya is not subject to specific travel restrictions, although visitors are urged to stay alert, follow local security advice and avoid political gatherings or demonstrations that can flare up with little warning. Insurance, Health Rules and Practical Impacts on Travellers One of the most immediate consequences for British holidaymakers is the link between the FCDO warning and travel insurance. The UK government’s advice explicitly notes that travel insurance may be invalidated if travellers enter areas where it advises against all travel or all but essential travel. This means trips that include overland routes close to the Somali or Ethiopian borders, or extensions into affected counties, may no longer be covered by standard policies. The change coincides with new Kenyan rules on visitor health coverage. Entry‑requirements pages for Kenya state that from 5 October 2026, most foreign travellers staying for less than 12 months must hold Kenya‑approved travel health insurance issued through a government‑linked platform. Foreign insurance policies, including UK‑based ones, are not accepted as a substitute for this mandatory local cover, although they remain important for broader benefits such as cancellation, evacuation and baggage. Travellers planning safaris or beach stays are being advised by tour operators and online industry briefings to double‑check that their itineraries do not pass through newly restricted areas and to confirm with insurers that planned routes remain insurable. For those considering road trips in northern Kenya, publicly available guidance emphasizes the importance of sticking to main highways, avoiding unscheduled stops near sensitive border stretches and coordinating closely with reputable local operators. The updated advisory may also influence pricing and availability. Some reports from the travel trade indicate that a small number of overland expeditions and cross‑border circuits involving Ethiopia are being reviewed or rerouted, while mainstream safari lodges in central and southern Kenya continue to operate normally ahead of the Christmas peak. How the UK Advice Compares With Other Countries’ Warnings The UK move comes as several other governments maintain elevated but stable advisories on Kenya. The United States currently lists Kenya at “Level 3: Reconsider travel,” citing risks linked to terrorism, crime, kidnapping, civil unrest and road safety. Its advisory highlights many of the same higher‑risk areas in the north‑east and along the Somali border, while acknowledging that key tourism corridors remain open. Advisory trackers that collate warnings from the UK, US, Canada and Australia show that all four governments currently differentiate sharply between Kenya’s main tourism belt and insecure border regions. While language and grading systems differ, the broad pattern is consistent: strong caution near Somalia and parts of the northern and coastal periphery, coupled with more routine advice for Nairobi and established safari and beach destinations. In Europe and Asia, publicly available notices from individual foreign ministries vary in tone, but many echo concerns about terrorism and localised instability while stopping short of blanket bans. Industry analysts note that Kenya’s position as a major African hub for aviation, safari tourism and business travel means that governments tend to calibrate warnings carefully, seeking to balance security messaging with recognition of the country’s importance as a regional gateway. Travel‑risk mapping published by commercial security firms and insurance providers generally aligns with the UK’s approach, showing a patchwork of higher‑risk areas concentrated along the Somalia frontier, parts of the northern corridor and some sections of the coast, set against moderate risk ratings in Nairobi and the main tourist heartlands. What UK Travellers Should Do Now For British visitors with upcoming trips, the latest change underscores the need to monitor official advisories regularly in the weeks before departure. The FCDO updates its Kenya guidance frequently, and archived versions show that wording around specific regions and border tensions can shift within days. Travellers are encouraged by airlines, tour operators and insurance documents to read the full country advice, not just headline warnings, so they understand which counties and roads are affected and how the guidance might relate to their planned route. Those who booked packages that include restricted areas may need to discuss amendments or alternative arrangements with their providers. Prospective visitors who remain within the main safari circuits and coastal resorts continue to book trips, according to trade press reports, but many are building extra flexibility into their plans. This can include fully refundable fares, accommodation with lenient cancellation terms and comprehensive insurance that covers trip disruption linked to changing government advice. With Kenya preparing for its busiest travel months from December through March, the UK advisory shift is unlikely to halt tourism altogether. However, it is expected to steer more British travellers toward well‑established routes and operators and away from self‑drive expeditions or exploratory itineraries that brush against the country’s most fragile border zones. Zonal security leaders report that persistent armed incursions continue to jeopardize agrarian and pastoral livelihoods along the regional administrative boundary. Authorities attribute this instability to security vacuums left by collapsed government administrative structures in neighboring West Guji Zone, allowing armed groups to conduct unimpeded raids. Burji Zone Police Commander Inspector Zemede Bantore stated that armed forces entering from West Guji have launched organized, heavy-weapons assaults on local farming communities. These attacks have caused civilian fatalities, livestock looting, property destruction, and mass displacement across border kebeles. Inspector Zemede explained that security deteriorated after federal defense forces redeployed from front-line border posts to northern operational theaters, leaving local security forces overwhelmed. Without federal defense reinforcements, Burji authorities have initiated traditional mediation using local elder networks and the Geda system. The strategy aims to establish dialogue between Burji elders and West Guji community leaders to restrain local youth and prevent armed groups—identified by authorities as OLF-Shene and organized local “Fole” formations—from crossing zonal boundaries. In contrast, Chief Inspector Sidama Madamo, Head of the Kore Zone Police Department, stated that local security conditions in Kore Zone remain unfavorable for community-level mediation. Because local administrative structures in neighboring border districts like Gelana are largely non-functional, Kore officials rely on joint security directives from consultations with regional police commissions, regional peace and security offices, and federal military leadership. While regional special forces provide limited security support in Kore Zone, Burji officials emphasized that their jurisdiction operates without regional special force reinforcement. Both zonal police leaderships have reiterated calls for immediate federal security intervention and permanent troop deployments to secure agricultural zones and restore stability for border populations. __ Join our Telegram Channel : t.me/borkena Like borkena on Facebook Ethiopian Sports News Join the conversation. Regional security officials report that armed incursions are threatening local agrarian and pastoral livelihoods, exacerbated by the collapse of government structures in West Guji. somalia.title: From Muscat to Mogadishu: Oman’s Diplomatic and Commercial Push in Somalia - FTL Somalia
somalia.content: From Muscat to Mogadishu: Oman's Diplomatic and Commercial Push in Somalia - Somali News today Live Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors International Relations Nationwide From Muscat to Mogadishu: Oman’s Diplomatic and Commercial Push in Somalia November 7, 2026 5 min read MOGADISHU , Prime Minister Hamza Abdi Barre met with Oman’s new Ambassador to Somalia, Salim bin Habib Al-Amri, on Saturday to discuss strengthening the historical ties between the two countries and expanding cooperation in economic, trade, and transport sectors. The meeting focused on the importance of maritime corridors, facilitating the movement of transport and goods, and enhancing connectivity between ports and commercial exchange, with the aim of creating shared economic opportunities that serve the interests of both nations. The Prime Minister underscored the importance Somalia attaches to strengthening its friendly relations and strategic cooperation with the Sultanate of Oman. Ambassador Al-Amri expressed his gratitude for the warm reception and stressed the significance of the historical relations and mutual cooperation between the two countries. The meeting is the latest in a series of high-level engagements that have accelerated since Oman reopened its embassy in Mogadishu in October 2026, ending a 36-year absence, as FTL Somalia reported on the trade talks that followed the reopening . A Relationship Rebuilt on Trade and Investment The Prime Minister’s meeting follows months of deepening economic engagement. In April 2026, Somalia’s Foreign Minister visited Muscat for talks with the Oman Investment Authority, where the two sides explored opportunities in energy, infrastructure, logistics, food security, and information technology. Omani officials have also expressed interest in Somalia’s Al-Ula Special Economic Zone, with the Omani Authority for Investment Promotion and Export Development offering technical expertise and training to zone management staff. The trade relationship, while growing, remains modest. Bilateral goods trade reached approximately $538 million in 2025, up from $429 million in 2022, with Oman maintaining a surplus of about $108 million. Oman’s exports to Somalia include dairy products, milling products, and salt, while Somalia’s exports to Oman have also increased in recent years. As the Commerce Minister’s earlier meeting with the Omani ambassador highlighted, the relationship is real but still far from its potential. The two countries have also engaged on transport connectivity. Oman’s Minister of Transport, Communications and Information Technology led a delegation to Mogadishu for talks with Somali counterparts on enhancing cooperation in transport and investment opportunities. The Omani delegation included officials from the Public Authority for Special Economic Zones and Free Zones, the Oman Investment Authority, Oman Airports, and other entities, signaling a comprehensive approach to the relationship. The diplomatic momentum has been building for over a year. In June 2025, the Somali and Omani ambassadors to Tanzania met in Dar es Salaam to reaffirm bilateral ties and explore new avenues for cooperation in trade, regional stability, and development, as FTL Somalia reported on the diplomatic engagement . The Strategic Logic For Somalia, the relationship with Oman offers several advantages. Oman has consistently supported Somalia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, including its rejection of any entities outside the framework of the Somali state. That support is valuable in a region where Somalia’s territorial integrity faces challenges, particularly from Israel’s recognition of Somaliland and the UAE’s deep ties with Hargeisa. As Mogadishu has worked to counter the Israel-UAE campaign to secure recognition for Somaliland, Oman’s diplomatic stance has been a reliable counterweight. Oman’s geographic position on the Arabian Peninsula, adjacent to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean, makes it a natural maritime partner for Somalia. Omani ports and logistics networks serve as a conduit for Somali trade with the wider Gulf and Asian markets, and the two countries share deep historical, cultural, and commercial ties rooted in Indian Ocean trade networks that linked Mogadishu and Berbera to Muscat and Salalah long before the modern state system. The livestock trade has been a particular focus. In 2023, Somalia exported 150,000 goats to Gulf countries, including Oman, through Bosaso Port, as FTL Somalia reported on the livestock exports . Somaliland has also been working to facilitate livestock exports to Oman, with preparations underway to meet international standards and ensure animal health certification systems are robust, as the region’s livestock minister briefed his cabinet . The two countries have also signed a livestock trade agreement aimed at strengthening veterinary standards and facilitating exports. Critical Note The Prime Minister’s meeting with Ambassador Al-Amri is a routine diplomatic engagement, and it should be reported as such. What matters is not the photo opportunity but whether the commercial promises that have accompanied the reopening of Oman’s embassy translate into measurable outcomes. The trade figures suggest a relationship that is real but limited. $538 million in annual goods trade is meaningful for Somalia, particularly given its narrow export base, but it is a fraction of what a functioning commercial relationship between two Indian Ocean states could generate. Oman’s interest in Somalia’s fisheries, livestock, and blue economy is welcome, but expressions of interest are not investment. The Al-Ula Special Economic Zone has attracted Omani attention, but no anchor investment has materialized. The strategic dimension is more significant than the economic one at this stage. Oman’s consistent support for Somalia’s territorial integrity, and its refusal to follow Israel’s path on Somaliland, gives Mogadishu a reliable partner in the Gulf. That support is valuable, but it is not a substitute for the kind of commercial engagement that creates jobs and generates revenue. The test of the Oman relationship will be whether the embassy in Mogadishu becomes a hub for business facilitation, whether Omani investment materializes in the fisheries and livestock sectors, and whether Somali exporters gain access to Omani ports and markets on terms that benefit both sides. Until those things happen, the meetings and the memoranda will remain what they are: diplomacy, not development. somalia.summary: Oman is enhancing its diplomatic and commercial ties with Somalia, as evidenced by a recent meeting between Somali Prime Minister Hamza Abdi Barre and Oman's Ambassador Salim bin Habib Al-Amri. This engagement aims to strengthen historical relations and expand cooperation in trade, transport, and economic sectors, particularly focusing on maritime corridors to facilitate goods movement. Since reopening its embassy in Mogadishu in October 2026 after a 36-year absence, Oman has expressed interest in Somalia's Al-Ula Special Economic Zone and various sectors, including energy and logistics. Despite a modest increase in bilateral trade, reaching approximately $538 million in 2025, the relationship remains underdeveloped compared to its potential. Oman’s support for Somalia's sovereignty is crucial, especially amid regional challenges. The success of this partnership will depend on translating diplomatic engagements into tangible investments and job creation, particularly in fisheries and livestock, which are vital for Somalia's economy.

somalia.title: Somalia warns of growing military cooperation between Yemen’s Houthis and Al-Shabaab - Horseed Media
somalia.content: Somalia warns of growing military cooperation between Yemen's Houthis and Al-Shabaab | Horseed Media Skip to content Search Home Somalia News Puntland News World News in English Featured More.. Dowladda Federaalka Galmudug Hiiraan News Jubaland News Koonfur Galbeed SSC Somaliland Follow us Search News Somalia Somalia warns of growing military cooperation between Yemen’s Houthis and Al-Shabaab Posted by: Horseed Staff Somalia’s federal government has warned of increasing military and technical cooperation between Yemen’s Houthi movement and the Al-Qaeda-linked militant group Al-Shabaab, raising concerns that the partnership could strengthen the group’s capacity to carry out more sophisticated attacks. 7 November, 2026 Share Tweet Somali officials say the alleged cooperation could provide Al-Shabaab with access to advanced military expertise, particularly in drone technology and weapons development, potentially increasing the threat to civilians and government forces. Ali Mohamed Omar, Somalia’s Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, known as Ali Bal’ad, raised the concerns in an interview with TRT World. He said that although the Houthis and Al-Shabaab have different ideologies and political objectives, the two groups appear to cooperate in technical and specialised areas. The minister warned that any military or technical assistance from the Yemeni movement could significantly enhance Al-Shabaab’s operational capabilities. He said the Somali militant group currently has limited technical expertise, but access to advanced knowledge of drones and weapons could enable it to plan and execute more complex attacks. Such developments, he added, would pose a serious threat to civilian lives and increase the security burden on Somalia’s government. Concerns over weapons trafficking and technical support Ali Bal’ad said Yemen had long served as a route for the smuggling of illicit weapons into Somalia. He stressed that the arms-trafficking networks predated the emergence of the Houthi movement. However, he said the situation had become more concerning amid reports that relations between the two groups may have expanded beyond weapons trafficking to include technical and military cooperation. The warnings come amid growing scrutiny of links between armed groups operating across the Red Sea and the wider Horn of Africa region. A February 2026 report by the Somali research institute Seldg examined the relationship between the Houthis and Al-Shabaab, concluding that their cooperation had evolved beyond initial logistical and intelligence exchanges. According to the report, the relationship now includes political, media and military dimensions. Hussein Sheikh-Ali, the report’s author and a former national security adviser to the Somali president, told The Africa Report in an interview published on 17 February that the relationship had become increasingly organised and systematic. He said what had previously been largely limited to meeting mutual needs and facilitating arms trafficking had developed into a more structured pattern of cooperation, raising concerns about regional security. Drone technology raises security concerns The Seldg report said contacts between the two groups initially involved intelligence sharing and the facilitation of maritime operations. These interactions subsequently developed into logistical and technical cooperation, according to the findings. The report also cited confidential sources who had provided information to the United Nations Panel of Experts on Yemen, alleging that the Houthis were training Al-Shabaab members in drone technology and the manufacture of explosive devices. The alleged training reportedly covers both improvised and more sophisticated explosive systems. Concerns about Al-Shabaab’s potential access to drone technology were also raised in a United Nations report published in October 2025. The report highlighted the possibility that members of the group could receive training to use drones in offensive operations. Al-Shabaab has previously used unmanned aerial technology primarily for reconnaissance and surveillance, but the acquisition of more advanced technical skills could potentially allow it to expand its use of drones in attacks. The development would represent a further security challenge for Somalia, which has spent years fighting the militant group and attempting to restore stability across the country. The reported links between the Houthis and Al-Shabaab have also raised wider concerns about the security implications of growing cooperation among armed groups across the Red Sea, particularly given the region’s importance to international shipping and maritime trade. Officials warn that this partnership could enhance Al-Shabaab's capabilities, particularly in drone technology and weapons development, posing a greater threat to civilians and government forces. Ali Mohamed Omar, Somalia’s Minister of State for Foreign Affairs, highlighted that despite differing ideologies, the two groups are collaborating in technical areas. Facebook Instagram X VKontakte Youtube Somali Guardian News Somalia Africa World Featured Editor Picks Editorials Home News Somalia Somalia chief justice says president threatens his security after court ruling Somalia chief justice says president threatens his security after court ruling November 7, 2026 Share Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – Somalia’s Chief Justice, Bashe Yusuf Ahmed, said on Saturday that he no longer felt safe in the capital, Mogadishu, alleging that his personal security was threatened by President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud. “I do not feel safe in the capital of the Somali nation. My security is threatened by the president whose term the court ruled had expired,” Bashe told journalists during a press briefing. His remarks followed his dismissal by President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud on Wednesday. However, five other Supreme Court judges subsequently ruled that the president’s term had expired, his constitutional amendments were unlawful and his decision to dismiss the chief justice was without legal authority. Since the ruling, all five judges, together with the chief justice, have reportedly faced security threats, while troops have taken control of the Supreme Court building in Mogadishu. The chief justice and the five judges have since sought refuge at the residence of former President Sharif Sheikh Ahmed, following the authorities’ decision to withdraw the chief justice’s security detail, as well as the security personnel assigned to the five judges who issued the ruling. In an emotional statement, Bashe questioned how ordinary Somali citizens could feel secure in Mogadishu if even senior state officials were unable to enjoy personal security in the capital. He further questioned how officials from other parts of the country could reasonably expect to find safety there. He lamented that, in present-day Mogadishu, only those who wield weapons could feel secure. Despite the circumstances, Bashe expressed hope for a brighter future, saying that Somalia would one day see justice prevail and that those who wield weapons and those who do not would stand on equal footing before the law. During a press briefing, Bashe stated that he felt threatened by the president, particularly after his dismissal by Mohamud, which was later ruled unlawful by five Supreme Court judges. These judges also faced security threats after the ruling, leading them and Bashe to seek refuge at the home of former President Sharif Sheikh Ahmed. somalia.title: Somalia plunged deeper into political crisis after Supreme Court rules presidential term extension unlawful - Horseed Media
somalia.content: Somalia plunged deeper into political crisis after Supreme Court rules presidential term extension unlawful | Horseed Media Skip to content Search Home Somalia News Puntland News World News in English Featured More.. Dowladda Federaalka Galmudug Hiiraan News Jubaland News Koonfur Galbeed SSC Somaliland Follow us Search News Somalia Somalia plunged deeper into political crisis after Supreme Court rules presidential term extension unlawful Posted by: Mohamed Osman Residents of Mogadishu have expressed sharply divided views after Somalia’s Supreme Court ruled that an extension of President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s term in office was unconstitutional, deepening an already tense political standoff in the country. 7 November, 2026 Share Tweet The ruling, delivered on Thursday, has intensified tensions between the government and opposition groups, with accusations of interference in the judiciary and concerns over the country’s constitutional order. Some residents welcomed the court’s decision, arguing that respect for the rule of law is essential to democratic governance. “The Supreme Court is right and its decision is right. In the world, all people and governments abide by court decisions, and the rule of law must be respected,” Mogadishu resident Abdullahi Hassan Sheikh said. However, others questioned the court’s position. “I see the court decision as wrong because, when the new constitution was being approved, the court was operational,” said another resident, Mohamed Farah Ahmed. Dispute over presidential mandate Somalia has been gripped by a deepening political crisis, with opposition figures accusing President Mohamud of attempting to consolidate power through constitutional reforms. The president has sought to move the country towards a fully democratic electoral system, replacing the longstanding clan-based arrangement under which traditional elders select representatives. However, his opponents have rejected the proposed changes, describing them as a political power grab. The dispute escalated after Mohamud declared a transition period that effectively extended his presidency by one year following the expiration of his mandate in May. The president has maintained that constitutional amendments approved by parliament authorised him to remain in office while preparations continued for Somalia’s first nationwide democratic elections, scheduled for April and May 2027. But the Supreme Court ruled on Thursday that the amendments could not be applied retrospectively to the president’s current term, meaning he should have left office in May. The court called on political parties to reach a new agreement within 30 days and urged that elections be held within 90 days. Tensions between president and judiciary The dispute took a further turn when the president’s office announced on Facebook that Chief Justice Bashe Yusuf Ahmed had been dismissed and that a replacement had been appointed. The announcement, made before the court’s ruling had been formally published, cited concerns about the need for an efficient and fair judiciary. The Supreme Court rejected the move, arguing that the president had no constitutional authority to remove the chief justice. It accused Mohamud of attempting “to obstruct the administration of justice in the constitutional case filed before the Supreme Court”. Former Prime Minister Hassan Ali Khaire subsequently accused the president of launching an assault on the judiciary and deploying troops to the court’s premises on Thursday. He further alleged that the chief justice and lawyers were being pursued at their homes for arrest, subjected to torture, and that the court’s operations had been suspended. The allegations could not be independently verified by AFP. However, images published by Somali media purportedly showed military personnel inside the court’s compound. “Somalia stands at a dangerous juncture. The dismantling of our judiciary is a direct threat to the rule of law,” Khaire said. He called on Somalis across the country to defend constitutional governance. Political divisions and security challenges The constitutional dispute has exposed longstanding divisions within Somalia’s political establishment. Most opposition groups and regional administrations boycotted the parliamentary vote on constitutional amendments in March, with some claiming they had been prevented from participating. The disagreements later spilled onto the streets, with violent clashes between rival political factions reported in Mogadishu in June. The political instability comes as Somalia continues to battle the Al-Qaeda-linked militant group Al-Shabaab, which maintains control over parts of the country and has waged an insurgency against the government for years. The security situation has been further complicated by declining international support for the military campaign against the group. International donors have expressed frustration over the limited progress against the militants and persistent political divisions, prompting reductions in funding for the African Union-led military mission, which has been operating in Somalia for almost two decades. Uganda, the largest troop contributor to the African Union force, announced this week that it would withdraw all its troops by the end of 2027. Meanwhile, Washington has cut its financial contributions to a key United Nations logistics operation supporting the military coalition. With political tensions escalating, international assistance under pressure and the fight against Al-Shabaab continuing, Somalia faces mounting challenges to its political stability and security. The Supreme Court’s ruling has added another layer of uncertainty, raising questions about the country’s leadership, the independence of its judiciary and the future of its planned democratic transition. The ruling has intensified tensions between the government and opposition groups, with accusations of judicial interference and concerns over constitutional integrity. While some residents support the court's decision as a necessary affirmation of the rule of law, others criticize it, arguing that the court was operational during the approval of the new constitution. The president's declaration of a transition period to extend his presidency has been met with resistance, as opponents view it as a power grab. The Supreme Court has called for political parties to reach a new agreement within 30 days and urged elections within 90 days. The situation has escalated further with the president's dismissal of the Chief Justice, which the court rejected, leading to accusations of an assault on the judiciary. Dowladda Federaalka Galmudug Hiiraan News Jubaland News Koonfur Galbeed SSC Somaliland Follow us Search News Somalia Somalia: Security Tensions Escalate in Beledweyne as Military Forces Deploy Near Traditional Leader’s Residence Posted by: Horseed Staff BELEDWEYNE, Somalia — Security tensions have escalated in Beledweyne, the capital of Somalia’s Hiiraan region, amid the presence of Hirshabelle Vice President Abdifatah Hassan Afrah, opposition politicians, and traditional leader Ugaas Yusuf Ugaas Hassan Ugaas. 7 November, 2026 Share Tweet Somali National Army (SNA) troops and National Intelligence and Security Agency (NISA) personnel have reportedly arrived at the residence of Ugaas Yusuf Ugaas Hassan. The development follows a statement he made last night urging members of his clan serving on the front lines to withdraw from their positions, as tensions between the Hirshabelle administration and the people of Hiiraan continue to intensify. The latest reports indicate that a group of NISA personnel who defected earlier this morning and moved to the traditional leader’s residence have taken control of Beledweyne Airport. They have reportedly issued warnings to aircraft and anyone seeking to use the airport, as federal-level delegations are expected to arrive in the city to help resolve the escalating crisis. Former NISA Director Abdullahi Mohamed Ali, widely known as Sanbaloolshe, has also arrived in Beledweyne from Ethiopia. Following meetings with local politicians and business leaders from Hiiraan, Sanbaloolshe reportedly declared that Hirshabelle would no longer be allowed to operate in parts of Hiiraan, particularly in Beledweyne. Meanwhile, Djiboutian military officers stationed in the Hiiraan region are undertaking efforts to bring the opposing sides together in an attempt to resolve the dispute and prevent a possible armed confrontation. The situation remains tense as political and security developments continue to unfold in the regional capital, with efforts underway to prevent further escalation. somalia.title: Somalia's judicial independence under attack: Supreme Court chief warns of threats to his life as armed forces reportedly seize court - Sunatimes.com
somalia.content: Somalia's judicial independence under attack: Supreme Court chief warns of threats to his life as armed forces reportedly seize court Home About Us Quran Investigative Reports Latest News Featured Items Articles Contact Us ALSO IN THE NEWS Somalia's judicial independence under attack: Supreme Court chief warns of threats to his life as armed forces reportedly seize court 0 Saturday November 07, 2026 - 19:07:00 in Latest News by Super Admin Visits: 608 (Rating 0.0/5 Stars) Total Votes: 0 0 0 Share via Social Media Somalia's judicial independence under attack: Supreme Court chief warns of threats to his life as armed forces reportedly seize court Somalia is facing an alarming constitutional and judicial crisis following reports that armed security forces loyal to former presidential term-holder Hassan Sheikh Mohamud have taken control of the Supreme Court, allegedly threatening the safety of Share Somalia is facing an alarming constitutional and judicial crisis following reports that armed security forces loyal to former presidential term-holder Hassan Sheikh Mohamud have taken control of the Supreme Court, allegedly threatening the safety of its Chief Justice and interfering with the country's highest judicial institution. The reported intervention follows a landmark Supreme Court ruling declaring that Hassan Sheikh Mohamud's constitutional presidential term had expired. The developments raise serious concerns about judicial independence, the separation of powers, constitutional governance and the personal security of Somalia's senior judges. SUPREME COURT CHIEF WARNS HIS LIFE IS IN DANGER According to statements attributed to the Chief Justice of Somalia's Supreme Court, his personal safety has been placed at serious risk following the court's ruling on the presidential term. The Chief Justice reportedly warned that armed forces had taken control of the court premises, creating an environment of intimidation and undermining the institution's ability to operate independently. If substantiated, these actions would represent an extraordinary escalation in the confrontation between the executive authorities and the judiciary. ALLEGATIONS OF CYBERATTACKS AND INTELLIGENCE INTERFERENCE The crisis has also extended into the digital infrastructure of Somalia's judicial system. The Chief Justice has reportedly alleged that the Supreme Court's electronic systems were compromised and that unauthorized actors gained control of the institution's digital operations. Further allegations suggest that Somalia's National Intelligence and Security Agency (NISA) took control of the Supreme Court's official Facebook presence. These allegations raise urgent questions about possible cyber interference, unauthorized access to judicial information and attempts to silence the court's institutional communications. Waagacusub Media has not independently established the technical origin of the alleged cyber intrusion or verified NISA's responsibility. WAAGACUSUB JOURNALISTS REPORT ARMED PERSONNEL INSIDE THE COURT Waagacusub Media journalists have reported witnessing armed personnel occupying areas of the Supreme Court premises in Mogadishu. According to their firsthand observations, armed men were seen openly chewing khat, locally known as miraa , inside the judicial compound. The journalists also reported the apparent removal or exclusion of independent judicial personnel from the premises. These eyewitness accounts, if corroborated, would indicate a disturbing breakdown in the security and institutional independence of Somalia's highest court. A Supreme Court must remain a place where judges administer justice without coercion, not a facility controlled through armed intimidation. UN HUMAN RIGHTS EXPERT CALLS FOR RESPECT FOR JUDICIAL INDEPENDENCE Professor Ben Saul, the United Nations Special Rapporteur on human rights and counter-terrorism, has publicly called on Somalia's leadership to respect the independence of the Supreme Court, constitutional procedures and presidential term limits. His intervention comes amid mounting concerns over the country's constitutional dispute. Although UN Special Rapporteurs are independent experts and their statements do not automatically constitute the institutional position of the United Nations, his warning carries significant international human rights implications. The reported threats against judicial officials and allegations of interference with the Supreme Court demand urgent scrutiny by competent national and international authorities. A DIRECT CHALLENGE TO CONSTITUTIONAL GOVERNANCE The Supreme Court's reported determination that Hassan Sheikh Mohamud's presidential mandate had expired lies at the centre of the current confrontation. However, the legal validity and enforceability of the ruling, together with the competing constitutional interpretations, must be assessed through lawful judicial procedures rather than coercion. No political leader, security institution or intelligence agency should be permitted to substitute armed force for constitutional adjudication. Any attempt to intimidate judges, unlawfully occupy court facilities or interfere with judicial communications would constitute a grave threat to the rule of law. URGENT CALL FOR INTERNATIONAL SCRUTINY The developments warrant immediate attention from the United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, relevant UN Special Procedures, international diplomatic partners and organizations defending judicial independence. Waagacusub Media calls for: An independent investigation into the reported armed takeover of the Supreme Court. Immediate protection for the Chief Justice, judges, judicial staff and their families. An independent digital forensic investigation into the alleged compromise of the court's systems and official social media accounts. Verification of the legal authority under which armed personnel entered and remained inside the judicial compound. Restoration of unrestricted, lawful judicial operations and accountability for any proven intimidation or unlawful interference. The allegations concerning the involvement of NISA and forces associated with Hassan Sheikh Mohamud require independent investigation. Responsibility must be established through credible evidence rather than political accusation alone. SOMALIA'S CONSTITUTIONAL FUTURE AT A CRITICAL CROSSROADS The independence of the judiciary is not a privilege granted by a president. It is a fundamental safeguard against arbitrary power. If armed forces can occupy the Supreme Court following an adverse constitutional ruling, the consequences would extend far beyond a dispute over presidential tenure. They would threaten the ability of every Somali citizen to seek justice without political interference. A nation cannot claim constitutional government while its highest court operates under the shadow of armed intimidation. The international community must not overlook credible threats against judicial institutions or the individuals entrusted with defending constitutional order. Waagacusub Media will continue documenting developments, seeking independent corroboration and examining allegations of political interference, security-force intimidation and cyberattacks against Somalia's judiciary. WAAGACUSUB MEDIA Independent Investigative Journalism | Somalia Editorial note: This report distinguishes the Supreme Court's reported ruling, statements attributed to the Chief Justice, Waagacusub journalists' eyewitness accounts and allegations that remain independently unverified. The accused authorities' responses have not been established for this article. No Comments yet... somalia.title: Mogadishu’s Balancing Act: CEN-SAD, Western Sahara, and the Cost of Aligning With Algeria - FTL Somalia
somalia.content: Mogadishu's Balancing Act: CEN-SAD, Western Sahara, and the Cost of Aligning With Algeria - Somali News today Live Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors International Relations Nationwide Mogadishu’s Balancing Act: CEN-SAD, Western Sahara, and the Cost of Aligning With Algeria November 7, 2026 6 min read TRIPOLI , Somalia’s Foreign Minister Abdisalam Abdi Ali attended the 22nd session of the Community of Sahel-Saharan States (CEN-SAD) in Tripoli on Saturday, a diplomatic engagement that comes just days after Mogadishu cast a controversial vote at the UN Security Council on the disputed Western Sahara, aligning itself with Russia and against Morocco on a file where it had previously supported Rabat. The CEN-SAD summit focused on revitalizing the organization and strengthening cooperation on economic development, peace and security, health, and cultural exchange. Somalia’s participation signals its commitment to deepening ties across the Sahel, North Africa, and the Horn, a region where its diplomatic alignments are increasingly being tested. But the timing of the summit is notable. On October 30, Somalia abstained from a US-drafted resolution at the Security Council that would have renewed the mandate of the UN mission in Western Sahara (MINURSO) and placed Morocco’s autonomy plan at the center of negotiations. It then voted in favor of a rival Russian draft that simply extended the mission’s mandate without changes. The Russian draft received only three votes, from Russia, China, and Somalia, and was rejected. The Israel Factor Behind the Shift The vote marked a significant reversal for Mogadishu. In November 2025, Somalia’s foreign minister signed a cooperation agreement with his Moroccan counterpart , and in December 2025 Somalia publicly maintained neutrality on Western Sahara while backing UN-led peace efforts , a position widely read in Rabat as support for Resolution 2797 and the autonomy initiative. But Morocco’s deepening relationship with Israel through the Abraham Accords has become a source of concern for Mogadishu. In September 2026, Morocco and Israel announced they would upgrade their diplomatic missions to full embassies, a move that was explicitly framed as part of the Abraham Accords framework. This normalization is built on a quid pro quo: the United States and Israel recognize Morocco’s sovereignty over Western Sahara, and Morocco recognizes Israel. For Somalia, this is not an abstract diplomatic arrangement. Israel’s recognition of Somaliland in December 2025 was viewed in Mogadishu as a direct assault on Somalia’s territorial integrity , and President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud has warned that Israel is seeking to establish a military presence in the breakaway region and potentially resettle Palestinians there. The Somali government has framed Israel’s actions as part of a broader strategy to reshape the Red Sea and Horn of Africa, a concern that aligns with Algeria’s own opposition to Israeli influence in the region. Morocco, despite its own normalization with Israel, did publicly reject Israel’s recognition of Somaliland and expressed support for Somalia’s territorial integrity. But the contradiction is difficult to ignore. A country that is deepening its ties with Israel while Mogadishu views Israeli expansionism as an existential threat is not a reliable partner in Somalia’s eyes. Algeria, by contrast, has no such contradiction. It has no relations with Israel, and it has used international forums to defend Somalia’s sovereignty against Israeli encroachment. Algeria’s Expanding Footprint in Mogadishu Algeria’s courtship of Mogadishu has moved from rhetoric to institutional engagement over the past year. In May 2026, Somalia’s Interior Minister, Ali Yusuf Ali Hoosh, traveled to Algiers for security and counterterrorism talks with Algerian officials. Hoosh described Algeria as “a strategic partner and a steadfast supporter of Somalia’s sovereignty and stability,” and praised its “leading role in supporting African and Arab just causes”. The relationship has also been institutionalized at other levels. In February 2026, the two countries established a judicial cooperation agreement and moved to form a parliamentary friendship committee , extending the partnership into legal and legislative domains. Algeria has also invested in soft power: in December 2025, the first cohort of Somali students arrived in Algeria on scholarships , an initiative that Hoosh praised as “a real investment in human capital”. Algeria has also defended Somalia’s sovereignty on the international stage. In September 2026, Algiers used the UN General Assembly to accuse Israel of seeking to divide Somalia through its recognition of Somaliland. This diplomatic support is particularly valuable to Mogadishu because it comes from a country that shares its opposition to Israeli influence in the region, without the baggage of a normalization agreement with Tel Aviv. The opening of the Algerian embassy in Mogadishu has provided the institutional platform for this outreach. Algeria has also discussed cooperation in oil and gas exploration, offering Sonatrach’s expertise as Mogadishu prepares to launch exploration. The Cost of the Shift The CEN-SAD summit in Tripoli places Somalia in a forum where both Morocco and Algeria have influence. For Somalia, participation is a low-cost way to engage with a region that matters to its security and economic future, but it does not resolve the contradiction between its CEN-SAD commitments and its UN voting record. Morocco has been a consistent supporter of Somalia’s territorial integrity, including its opposition to Somaliland’s recognition. A public break on Western Sahara could strain that relationship at a time when Mogadishu can ill afford to lose allies. But the calculation in Mogadishu may be that Morocco’s support is compromised by its embrace of Israel. If Rabat is willing to recognize Israeli sovereignty over contested territory and accept Israeli support for its own claims, how reliable can its commitment to Somali sovereignty be? Critical Note Somalia’s vote at the Security Council was not a routine diplomatic maneuver. It was a public break with a country that has supported Somalia’s most sensitive national interest. But it was also a signal that Mogadishu is recalibrating its alliances in response to a changing regional landscape. The Israel factor is central to that recalibration. Morocco’s deepening ties with Israel through the Abraham Accords have made it an increasingly uncomfortable partner for a government that views Israeli expansionism as a direct threat. Algeria, which has no relations with Israel and has actively defended Somalia’s sovereignty against Israeli encroachment, offers a different kind of partnership. It is not without its own costs, Morocco will remember the vote, but it reflects a clear-eyed assessment of where Somalia’s interests lie. The Foreign Minister’s presence in Tripoli is a reminder that Somalia’s diplomatic dance is becoming more complex. The country is navigating a region where old alliances are shifting, new partnerships are forming, and the lines between friend and foe are being redrawn. The vote on Western Sahara was a statement. The CEN-SAD summit is a follow-through. Whether the strategy pays off will depend on whether Algeria can deliver the support it promises, and whether Morocco’s response is one of understanding or retribution. Whatsapp Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Co-operation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty met his Somali counterpart, Abdisalam Abdi Ali, on Saturday to discuss ways to strengthen bilateral relations and coordinate positions on regional issues of mutual concern. The meeting was held on the sidelines of the 22nd Ordinary Session of the Executive Council of the Community of Sahel-Saharan States (CEN-SAD) in Tripoli, Libya. Talks focused on expanding co-operation across various fields, particularly the economic, development and investment sectors, Foreign Ministry Spokesman Nader Zaki said. Abdelatty reaffirmed Egypt’s commitment to supporting efforts to build Somalia’s state institutions and strengthen their capabilities. He reiterated Cairo’s firm support for Somalia’s unity, sovereignty and territorial integrity. He also firmly rejected any unilateral measures that could undermine Somalia’s territorial integrity or infringe upon its sovereignty. The two ministers exchanged views on developments in the Horn of Africa. They stressed the importance of supporting national institutions and safeguarding the unity, sovereignty and territorial integrity of countries across the region. Abdelatty emphasised that responsibility for the security and management of the Red Sea rests exclusively with its littoral states. The two sides agreed to maintain co-ordination and build on the outcomes of the consultative Alamein Summit, hosted by Egypt last October, to support peace, stability and development in the region. In a separate meeting, Abdelatty held talks with Djiboutian Foreign Minister Abdoulkader Houssein Omar on ways to strengthen bilateral relations and discuss regional developments, particularly in Sudan, Somalia and the Red Sea. Abdelatty called for stronger co-operation among Red Sea littoral states to safeguard maritime security and ensure freedom of navigation. أحمد الخرطوم winwin أضفنا الى 'غوغل' كثف منتخب السودان استعداداته خلال معسكره القصير بالعاصمة كيغالي، تأهبًا لمواجهتي السنغال الحاسمتين، المقررتين يومي 12 و16 نوفمبر الجاري، ضمن الجولتين الثالثة والرابعة من المجموعة العاشرة في التصفيات المؤهلة لبطولة الأمم الأفريقية 2027 . وبدد طبيب المنتخب مخاوف الجماهير بعد تعرض حارس المرمى فريد مصطفى لعارض صحي طارئ استدعى نقله للمستشفى، فيما سيتلقى المدرب كواسي أبياه المزيد من الدعم بانضمام نجوم الهلال والمريخ للتدريبات. صفوف منتخب السودان تكتمل بانضمام نجوم العملاقين يلتحق نجوم الهلال والمريخ اليوم الجمعة 6 نوفمبر/ تشرين الثاني، بتدريبات "صقور الجديان" في العاصمة الرواندية كيغالي، بعد غيابهم عن الحصة التدريبية الأولى التي اقتصرت على المحترفين في الخارج واللاعبين الشباب الجدد في قائمة المدرب كواسي أبياه. ويسيطر نجوم العملاقين على قائمة مدرب السودان بوجود 19 لاعبًا يمثلون القوام الأساسي للمنتخب، في مشهد طبيعي لاستمرار الفريقين بالمنافسات المحلية والقارية، وكان المدرب قد منح الفرصة للاعبي الفريقين للمشاركة في مبارياتهما مؤخرًا بالدوري الرواندي، مفضلًا استمرارهم في التنافس الرسمي. اقرأ أيضًا بخطوة غريبة.. مدرب السودان يثير الجدل قبل مواجهتي السنغال مفاجآت وعائدون.. أبياه يكشف قائمة السودان لمواجهتي السنغال وفي سياق منفصل طمأن الطاقم الطبي الجماهير على الحالة الصحية لحارس المرمى الواعد فريد مصطفى، بعد أن تجاوز وعكة صحية طارئة استدعت نقله إلى المستشفى عقب الحصة التدريبية الأولى التي خاضها صقور الجديان. وأكد طبيب منتخب السودان محمد النعيم، في حديث للموقع الرسمي لاتحاد الكرة، سلامة اللاعب بناء على نتائج الفحوص، موضحًا أنه سيستأنف تدريباته مع زملائه بشكل طبيعي بعد حصوله على قسط قصير من الراحة. من جهة أخرى، سيخوض المنتخب السوداني 3 حصص تدريبية في ختام معسكره بكيغالي، قبل التوجه إلى داكار يوم 9 نوفمبر، استعدادًا لمواجهة السنغال يومي 12 و16 من الشهر ذاته، ضمن الجولتين الثالثة والرابعة من التصفيات الأفريقية؛ حيث يطمح المنتخب لتحقيق إهدار الفوز؟ الهلال السوداني الدوري السوداني الممتاز كرة قدم حافظ محمد أحمد الخرطوم winwin أضفنا الى 'غوغل' أحبط الهلال جماهيره وانقاد للتعادل بنتيجة 1-1 أمام نظيره رايون سبورت الرواندي، اليوم الأربعاء 4 نوفمبر، على ملعب "كيغالي بيليه" ضمن الجولة السابعة من الدوري الرواندي، الذي يشهد مشاركة الهلال ومواطنه المريخ . وفرط "الموج الأزرق" في فرصة تحقيق الفوز، مكتفيا بالتعادل بعد أن بادر بالتسجيل عبر قائده وهدافه محمد عبد الرحمن، قبل أن يدرك المنافس التعادل في الرمق الأخير من المباراة، ليهدر الفريق فرصة مثالية لتقليص الفارق مع صدارة الدوري، في انتظار خوض مبارياته المؤجلة الثلاث. مكاسب مضاعفة لـ"غربال" رغم تفريط الهلال في الفوز باستقباله هدف التعادل في اللحظات الأخيرة، إلا أن "الكابيتانو" محمد عبد الرحمن نجح في وضع فريقه بالمقدمة بهدف رائع، محققا مكاسب شخصية بتعزيز سجله التهديفي وتأكيد عودته القوية قبل المواجهات المرتقبة في مجموعات دوري أبطال أفريقيا عقب فترة التوقف الدولي. كما سيمنح مدرب المنتخب "كواسي أبياه" خياراً هجومياً مميزاً لاستعادة فاعلية "صقور الجديان" التهديفية، بخوضه مباراتين حاسمتين أمام المنتخب السنغالي بتصفيات بطولة الأمم الأفريقية. اقرأ أيضًا مدرب الهلال السوداني يكشف أزمة قاتلة قبل دوري أبطال أفريقيا رامي كمال: الهلال يستحق تكريمًا سياديًا وسنتوج باللقب القاري وسيحظى مدرب النادي الأزرق بفرصة مثالية لتجهيز عناصره عبر خوض تجارب ودية قوية خلال فترة التوقف الدولي، إذ سيلتحق 16 من أبرز نجومه بمنتخباتهم الوطنية، منهم 13 لاعبا في صفوف "صقور الجديان", و3 آخرون مع منتخبات بلدانهم. وسيعمل المدرب خلال هذا الغياب على إعداد البدائل، سعيا لتحقيق أفضل النتائج في دور المجموعات بدوري أبطال أفريقيا. وقرر المدرب جوزيف زينباور استغلال فترة التوقف بإجراء مباريات إعدادية، على أن يخوض الفريق مواجهة واحدة في الدوري الرواندي عقب التوقف، ليبدأ بعدها رحلة شاقة في دوري أبطال أفريقيا بملاقاة حوريا كوناكري الغيني في 28 نوفمبر الجاري، ثم يحل ضيفا على المغرب الفاسي في 5 فريقه أمام رايون سبورت الرواندي في الجولة السابعة من مسابقة الدوري الرواندي بالسيئة، مؤكدا أن فريقه فرط في فوز كان في المتناول بعد تقدمه المبكر، قبل التعهد بمعالجة السلبيات التي رافقت أداء الفريق في المباريات الأخيرة. وأوضح المدرب عبر مقطع فيديو نشره الموقع الرسمي للنادي، أنه لم يحظ بفرصة كافية لخوض تجارب ودية قبل انطلاقة الموسم للوقوف على إمكانات جميع اللاعبين، خاصة مع انضمام عناصر جديدة خلال فترة الانتقالات الصيفية، مشيرًا إلى أن فترة التوقف الدولي ستساعده في تجهيز الفريق بشكل أفضل. مدرب الهلال يشيد بنجميه كما أشاد زينباور بنجميه سفيان فريد و مصطفى كرشوم ، قائلا: "قدم الحارس سفيان مباراة متميزة، ويعد كرشوم مدافعا رائعا يمتاز بالهدوء والقدرة الفائقة على استخلاص الكرة وبناء اللعب". وأضاف: "تقدمنا مبكرا ولم نستثمر الفرص التي أتيحت لنا، واستقبلنا هدفا في الرمق الأخير من المباراة؛ كان يتعين علينا تسجيل هدفين على الأقل لنحسم المباراة، ولكننا لم نستثمر الفرص، علينا إيجاد حلول لاستقبال الأهداف المتأخرة، وبالمجمل، لست راضيا عن هذه النتيجة". اقرأ أيضًا رامي كمال: الهلال يستحق تكريمًا سياديًا وسنتوج باللقب القاري المريخ يربك تحضيرات الهلال لمجموعات دوري أبطال أفريقيا كما كشف زينباور عن أسباب تذبذب الأداء والتغييرات المستمرة في تشكيل فريقه مؤخرًا، قائلا: "لقد أضفنا عناصر جديدة خلال فترة الانتقالات، لدينا لاعبون شباب نرغب في منحهم فرصة المشاركة؛ لذا نجري هذه التعديلات لنقف على مستوياتهم، ونأمل أن يقدموا الإضافة المرجوة". وأضاف: "واجهنا منافسين أقوياء، على غرار فريق رايون الذي تميز باللياقة العالية والقوة البدنية، وسنواجه تحديات صعبة تستدعي وفرة في العناصر". وختم المدرب الألماني حديثه قائلاً: "نسعى لمزيد من التطور، ويتعين علينا مواصلة العمل الجاد لاستثمار الفرص في تطوير الجوانب البدنية والتكتيكية قبل المباريات الصعبة التي تنتظرنا في دوري أبطال أفريقيا ، إذ يجب أن نستعد جيدا لنبلغ مرحلة متميزة من الجاهزية حتى نتمكن من مجابهة التحديات المرتقبة". النشرة البريدية اشترك football.summary: كشف الألماني جوزيف زينباور، مدرب الهلال السوداني، عن أزمة تواجه فريقه قبل انطلاق دوري أبطال أفريقيا، بعد التعادل المخيب (1-1) أمام رايون سبورت الرواندي. وأشار زينباور إلى أن الفريق أضاع فرصة الفوز بعد تقدمه مبكرًا، مؤكدًا ضرورة معالجة السلبيات التي ظهرت في الأداء. وأوضح أنه لم يتمكن من إجراء تجارب ودية كافية قبل بداية الموسم، مما أثر على تقييم إمكانيات اللاعبين الجدد. وأعرب عن أمله في أن تساعد فترة التوقف الدولي في تحسين جاهزية الفريق. كما أشاد بأداء الحارس سفيان فريد والمدافع مصطفى كرشوم، مشددًا على أهمية استثمار الفرص وتفادي استقبال الأهداف المتأخرة. وأكد زينباور أن الفريق بحاجة إلى مزيد من التطور والعمل الجاد لمواجهة التحديات المقبلة في البطولة القارية.

football.summary: تستعد فرق بيراميدز والهلال السوداني لمواجهة مرتقبة في دوري أبطال أفريقيا 2026، حيث ستقام المباراة يوم السبت 19 ديسمبر 2026 في تمام الساعة 16:00. تعتبر هذه المباراة جزءًا من الموسم الحالي للبطولة، والتي تجمع بين أفضل الأندية الأفريقية. لم تبدأ المباراة بعد، ولكنها تثير اهتمام الجماهير، حيث يتطلع كل فريق لتحقيق الفوز وتعزيز موقفه في البطولة. في سياق آخر، تتوالى الأخبار الرياضية، حيث تم الإعلان عن جوائز الكرة الذهبية لعام 2026، مع تتويج هاري كين كأفضل لاعب في العالم، بينما حصل حكيمي على المركز الثالث عشر. كما شهدت الجوائز تكريمات أخرى، مثل جائزة "ياشين" لأفضل حارس، مما يعكس مستوى المنافسة العالي في عالم كرة القدم. تتابع الجماهير بشغف الأحداث الرياضية، مع توقعات مثيرة لمباراة بيراميدز والهلال السوداني.
